extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent owners, and petitioners (attorneys and agents) handling PTAB inter partes review, post‑grant review, and transitional business‑method post‑grant proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive rules, standards, and best‑practice guidance for initiating, defending, and conducting inter partes review (IPR), post‑grant review (PGR), and transitional business‑method post‑grant review proceedings before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB). Includes filing content, timing, evidence, motions, discovery, claim construction, estoppel, fees, and trial scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction requirement in Petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioners are required by the rules to construe the full breadth of each claim term in each challenged claim, even if not necessary to establish unpatentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO commentary applies the "broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification" standard: claim terms receive their plain meaning unless inconsistent with the specification. Detailed constructions only needed for terms that take on a special meaning in view of the specification. Alternative proposed constructions are permissible. For §112(f) (means/step‑plus‑function) limitations, the construction must identify specific portions of the specification that disclose the corresponding structure, material, or acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of patent owner prior statements
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner may submit statements of the patent owner filed in other proceedings before a federal court or the USPTO (but not the ITC) in which the owner took a position on claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such statements may be submitted with the Petition or separately, but the Board will consider them only after the trial has been instituted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold for instituting post‑grant review
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board will institute post‑grant review if the Petition, unrebutted, demonstrates that it is "more likely than not that at least one of the claims challenged in the Petition is unpatentable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO views this standard as harder to meet than the "reasonable likelihood" standard for IPR. The Board will take into account any Patent Owner Preliminary Response in determining whether the standard is met. The standard is applied claim‑by‑claim and ground‑by‑ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior presentation and institution
rubrics_metrics.description: The threshold for institution does not require "new issues"; a petitioner can meet the standard even if relying on art considered during original examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, the Board may consider prior presentation of substantially the same prior art or arguments in deciding whether to institute. Institution is claim‑by‑claim and ground‑by‑ground; proceedings are generally limited thereafter to those claims/issues unless supplemental information or claim amendments are filed. The Board may rarely institute based on a novel or unsettled legal question important to other patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing fees for post‑grant review petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Post‑grant review petition fees depend on the number of claims challenged: fee for up to 20 claims is $35,800; $800 for each claim over 20; no small/micro entity discount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent and multiple dependent claims are counted as in IPR. Fees may make PGR much more expensive than IPR or inter partes reexamination. USPTO indicated adopting a staged fee structure with limited subsidization in separate rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory estoppel for petitioners, real parties, and privies
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppel applies on a claim‑by‑claim basis after a final Board decision under the same standard as IPR: arguments "raised or reasonably could have been raised" during the proceeding are precluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because PGR permits broader grounds, estoppel likewise covers a broader range of arguments — after PGR final decision, petitioner, real parties, and privies are estopped from raising arguments based on §§101, 102, 103, 112 (except best mode), and/or 251 that were raised or reasonably could have been raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent owner estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owner estoppel provisions in post‑grant review mirror those in inter partes review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional post‑grant review availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitional PGR for business method patents permits PGR of certain business‑method patents under special rules; available as of Sept. 16, 2012, for eight years (no petitions after Sept. 15, 2020 absent legislation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no 9‑month‑from‑issue limitation for this program; it is only available when regular PGR would not otherwise be available (e.g., at any time for patents where PGR is completely unavailable). Procedural rules are the same as regular PGR and create the same estoppels, subject to available grounds limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may file transitional PGR petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: To file a Petition for transitional PGR for a business method patent, the petitioner's real party in interest or its privy must have been sued or charged with infringement of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish that it was "charged with infringement," the petitioner must demonstrate facts sufficient to establish standing for a declaratory judgment action in federal court (see cited Special Reports for details).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a "covered business method patent"
rubrics_metrics.description: A covered business method patent claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing or other operations used in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service, excluding patents for technological inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either method or apparatus claims can qualify; only one claim need qualify for the entire patent to be subject to transitional PGR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of "technological invention" for BPM eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a patent is for a technological invention, the USPTO will consider whether the claimed subject as a whole recites a technological feature that is novel and unobvious over the prior art and solves a technical problem using a technical solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims reciting a novel and nonobvious device or machine that performs a financial service will be considered technological; claims that merely recite known prior art technology or a predictable combination used in a normal way to perform a financial service will not be considered technological. Parties must sometimes address novelty and nonobviousness as threshold eligibility issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for challenging covered business method patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory bases for asserting unpatentability in transitional PGR are §§101, 102, 103, 112 (other than best mode), and 251, but with limits on pre‑AIA §§102/103 challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a Petition challenges a claim based on pre‑AIA §§102/103 (not AIA‑amended), such a challenge may only be based on prior art that (1) qualifies as prior art under pre‑AIA §102(a), or (2) disclosed the invention more than one year before the U.S. filing date and would qualify as pre‑AIA §102(a) prior art if another had disclosed it before the applicant's invention. Thus, U.S. sales/offers for sale under pre‑AIA §102(b) cannot be used; pre‑AIA §§102(d)–(g) are also unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel effect in federal court/ITC after transitional PGR
rubrics_metrics.description: For subsequent/federal court or ITC proceedings, estoppel from transitional PGR is narrower: the petitioner is estopped only from raising arguments actually raised and addressed in a final decision (not those that "reasonably could have been raised").

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors courts consider for stay of infringement action
rubrics_metrics.description: If seeking a stay of a corresponding infringement suit based on filing of a transitional PGR petition, courts consider: (1) whether a stay will simplify issues and streamline trial; (2) whether discovery is complete and a trial date set; (3) whether a stay would unduly prejudice the nonmoving party or give a clear tactical advantage; and (4) whether a stay will reduce litigation burden on parties and the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are non‑exclusive factors courts must consider when deciding a stay.

rubrics_metrics.name: General trial format and timing before the Board
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR, PGR, and transitional PGR are conducted entirely before the Board in a trial format; time from institution to final decision will generally be 12 months or less (six‑month extensions available but rarely used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During trial, petitioner must prove unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence (lower than clear and convincing in federal court); no presumption of patentability; claim construction uses the USPTO broadest reasonable construction standard (which may be broader than federal court claim construction). Federal Rules of Evidence generally govern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement and its effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may file a written settlement agreement and request termination of the trial at any time prior to final decision; the Board may facilitate or require settlement discussions and may, but is not required to, terminate the trial based on settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a trial is terminated before final decision (e.g., by settlement), estoppel provisions will not apply. A true copy of any settlement agreement must be filed with the USPTO and may be available to other federal agencies or persons on showing of good cause. The Board can still issue a final decision despite a filed settlement agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition content and strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Petition is the petitioner's principal brief and must establish the threshold standard for institution; it should, as much as possible, contain all fully developed arguments and all evidence available to support those arguments so the petition alone establishes unpatentability of challenged claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners should take great care before withholding arguments or evidence for supplemental information because discovery will mainly be used to rebut patent owner arguments, not to develop petitioner's own case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary Patent Owner Response (optional) — timing and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent owner may file an optional Preliminary Patent Owner Response no later than three months after the USPTO notice that the proceeding has been granted a filing date. The response must be limited to reasons why no trial should be instituted under 35 U.S.C. §314 (IPR) or §324 (PGR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page limits: 60 pages for IPR, 80 pages for PGR. The Preliminary Response may include evidence but new testimonial evidence only if in the "interests of justice." Examples of permissible arguments: statutory bar to review, asserted references not being prior art, prior art lacking a material limitation in all independent claims, prior art teaching away from proposed combination, petitioner's claim interpretation is unreasonable, brief §101 explanation, proceeding too complex to be completed within statutory time frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of Preliminary Patent Owner Response
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may elect to waive its right to file a Preliminary Patent Owner Response to expedite the Board's institution decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When waiver is filed, the Board may issue a determination on institution without waiting for the three‑month Preliminary Response period to expire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution notice limitations and rehearing
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Board institutes trial for at least one challenged claim, it will mail a Notice identifying the claims and issues upon which the trial is based; claims/grounds not included in the Notice will not be part of the trial (subject to supplemental information or amendments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party dissatisfied with inclusion/exclusion of a claim or ground may request rehearing. Institution is claim‑by‑claim and ground‑by‑ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling Order contents
rubrics_metrics.description: At institution, the Board issues a Scheduling Order setting due dates for trial events. It generally includes due dates for: (1) Patent Owner Response including motions to amend, (2) petitioner's reply and opposition to motion to amend, (3) patent owner's reply to opposition, (4) petitioner's motion for observation on cross‑examination testimony, motions to exclude, and requests for oral argument, (5) patent owner's replies/oppositions to motions to exclude, (6) replies to oppositions to motions to exclude, and (7) oral argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Scheduling Order is tailored to case facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary conference call expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board expects to initiate a conference call about one month after trial institution; parties can stipulate to different due dates except for the oral hearing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two days before the call, parties should provide a list of proposed motions and an outline of proposed claim amendments. Parties may later file motions not on the list, but the Board may require prior authorization and is unlikely to change due dates to accommodate late motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for filing supplemental information
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner may move to submit supplemental information under three alternative conditions: (1) request within one month after institution and supplemental info is relevant to a claim in the trial; (2) request after one month showing why info could not reasonably have been obtained earlier and that consideration is in the interests of justice; or (3) request at any time for info not relevant to instituted claims showing why it could not reasonably have been obtained earlier and that consideration is in the interests of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under alternative (1), petitioner can present information not included in the Petition regarding claims involved in the trial (including new patentability issues) without satisfying delay/interest‑of‑justice standards. Motions to submit supplemental info more than one month after institution for info relevant to instituted claims will be denied unless it could not reasonably have been obtained earlier; non‑relevant supplemental info is allowed only if it could not reasonably have been obtained within one month and is in the interests of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Owner Response (full) — timing, content, evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Owner Response must be filed within three months after the Notice of trial (unless the Board sets a different time), is treated as an opposition, and is subject to the same page limits as the Petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It should identify all involved claims believed to be patentable, explain the basis, and be filed with all supporting evidence (affidavits/declarations) and certified translations of non‑English documents. Unlike the Preliminary Response, the Patent Owner Response may include new testimonial evidence and other new evidence without Board authorization, and can expand arguments and evidence on issues that institution did not prevent the owner from addressing. The patent owner need only establish patentability by a preponderance of the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to amend the patent — requirements and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owner has a right to file one motion to amend after conferring with the Board; additional motions require Board authorization. Each motion must show: (1) support in the original disclosure for each amended/added claim; and (2) support in earlier disclosure for any benefit of earlier filing date sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motions to amend will not be authorized where the amendment does not respond to a ground involved in the trial, broadens claim scope, or introduces new matter. Motion and corresponding opposition each have 15‑page limits; proposed amendments are attachments that don't count toward page limits. Motions must be filed no later than the Patent Owner Response unless the Board sets a different deadline; late motions require good cause or Board authorization. Rules establish a rebuttable presumption that only one substitute claim is needed to replace each challenged claim and that the number of replacement claims must be "reasonable." Claim fees may be required if claim counts increase. The Board may deny a motion to amend without prejudice if original claims remain patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to motions to amend and evidentiary scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioners may oppose motions to amend without authorization and may submit evidence (e.g., expert declarations) directed to proposed substitute claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless otherwise agreed, petitioner's opposition to a motion to amend is limited to 15 pages and cannot be addressed in the Reply to the Patent Owner Response; parties should address briefing limits in the preliminary conference call.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioner's Reply limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner may file a Reply to the Patent Owner Response at a time set in the Scheduling Order, but the Reply may only respond to arguments raised in the Patent Owner Response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Reply raises a new issue or belatedly presents evidence, the entire Reply will not be considered and may be returned. Examples of new issues include new evidence necessary to make out a prima facie case for unpatentability of an original claim or evidence that could have been presented earlier. Reply page limit is 15 pages. Because of this constraint, petitioners should fully present and develop their arguments in the Petition and/or supplemental information; the Reply generally cannot cure defective Petition arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standards and admissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Rules of Evidence generally govern PTAB trial evidence. Evidence is submitted as exhibits in filings; expert opinion testimony that does not disclose underlying facts/data is given little to no weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits accompanying test data must explain why the test was performed, how data were used to determine results, and how the test is regarded in the relevant art. Testimony about patent law or examination practice will not be admitted. All non‑English documents relied upon must be translated into English and accompanied by an affidavit attesting to translation accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion practice form and content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Relief must be requested by motion. Generally, motions (other than timely patent owner motion to amend and specified motions) require Board authorization prior to filing. The moving party bears the burden to establish entitlement to the requested relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motions and oppositions are limited to 15 pages; replies to oppositions limited to 5 pages. Examples of motions: exclude evidence, seal, joinder, file supplemental information, judgment based on supplemental information, dismiss, observation on cross‑examination. The Board may require a pre‑motion notice specifying precise relief; failure to state sufficient basis may lead to denial without considering oppositions. Each motion must include: (1) statement of precise relief requested, (2) full statement of reasons including material facts, governing law, rules, and precedent, and may include (3) a separately numbered statement of material facts. Oppositions must comply with content requirements and need only identify material facts in dispute; any material fact not identified as disputed may be considered admitted. Moving party may file a reply limited to arguments raised in the opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory rulings and rehearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions may be decided interlocutorily before final decision; such interlocutory Board rulings are not final for judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party dissatisfied with an interlocutory ruling may request rehearing by the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Limited discovery is permitted at various times to develop the trial record. Three types of discovery are contemplated: mandatory initial disclosures, routine discovery, and additional discovery. Discovery periods will be set in the Scheduling Order, beginning with the patent owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may agree to different scopes of discovery and submit an agreement to the Board. All non‑English documents produced must be translated into English with an affidavit. For electronic discovery, the Practice Guide includes a model order governing e‑discovery specifying production manner and identification of emails by custodian and search terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory initial disclosures process
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may agree to mandatory initial disclosures and must submit their agreement to the Board no later than (1) the filing date of a Preliminary Patent Owner Response, or (2) if no Preliminary Response, the expiration of the time period for filing that response. After institution, initial disclosures must be filed "as soon as reasonably practicable" to permit related discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parties fail to agree, a party may seek mandatory initial disclosures by motion. Mandatory initial disclosures can proceed in one of two ways: the first, less‑extensive way is based on the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and requires disclosure of specified items (text truncated in source).
